12-1.inPlainWords: A sole proprietorship is not a separate legal person: its debts are your debts, and you pay them from personal assets. A company or LLP is separate, but that protection disappears if you sign a personal guarantee, mix personal and business money, or commit fraud. Unpaid share capital is capital of the company, not an immediate personal debt, though shareholders can be liable for unpaid calls and, on winding up, for the unpaid amount on their shares. Set your investment cap at an amount you can lose without missing a mortgage, rent or medical bill.
12-1.benefit: Losing money is not the only risk. In a sole proprietorship, business debts are recovered from the proprietor's personal assets. Partners in a general partnership are jointly and severally liable for partnership debts under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932. An LLP and a company are separate legal entities, so members' liability is normally limited to their agreed contribution; but a personal guarantee, a fraudulent transfer, or treating the company as an extension of yourself can make you personally liable. Under the Companies Act, 2013, a member remains liable for unpaid calls on shares, and a contributory is liable on winding up for the amount unpaid on shares.
12-1.caveats: “Money you can afford to lose” means an amount that won’t force you to sell your home or borrow from relatives. No reliable official Indian statistic on small-business survival rates was found, so no numerical figure is given here; only the legal consequences are described, which is why the evidence grade is B.
12-1.sources: Indian Contract Act, 1872. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Indian Partnership Act, 1932. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Companies Act, 2013 (sections 2(68), 45, 56). <https://www.mca.gov.in/>; Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>

12-2.inPlainWords: A personal guarantee makes you liable for the company's debt. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor's unless the contract limits it (section 128), and the creditor can usually proceed against the surety without first suing the company. A spouse who signs is personally liable to the extent of the guarantee; a spouse who does not sign is not liable merely because of the marriage. Both of you should treat a guarantee as a loan against your own home.
12-2.benefit: A guarantee is a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of default (Indian Contract Act, s.126). The creditor may generally enforce the guarantee without exhausting remedies against the company unless the contract says otherwise. A guarantee can be limited to a fixed amount, a fixed period, or a specific facility; a continuing guarantee can be revoked for future transactions by notice (s.130). Where two people guarantee the same debt, their liability is joint and several unless the contract says otherwise. Do not assume limited liability protects you once you have signed.
12-2.cost: Zero expense. When a bank, supplier or landlord asks for a personal guarantee, read the guarantee clause before signing. Ask for a cap on the amount and the period, and avoid an open-ended continuing guarantee. The hard part is refusing when the loan is conditional on your signature.
12-2.caveats: Most banks ask promoters of small companies to give personal guarantees. This section does not discourage borrowing; it asks you to understand what you are signing. Keep the guaranteed amount within the affordable-loss limit in item 1. A guarantee given by one spouse does not automatically bind the other; both are bound only if both sign or the debt is shown to be a joint family or partnership obligation. For negotiable instruments and guarantees, see Section 8, item 18.
12-2.sources: Indian Contract Act, 1872 (sections 126-147). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, Master Directions on loans and advances. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>

12-3.inPlainWords: A sole proprietorship and a general partnership carry unlimited personal liability: the proprietor or partners must pay business debts from personal assets. A limited liability partnership (LLP) and a company are separate legal persons, so members are normally liable only up to their agreed contribution. A private company needs at least two shareholders (one person may use a One Person Company). The protection depends on keeping personal and business finances separate.
12-3.benefit: Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, partners are jointly and severally liable for the firm's acts. An LLP under the LLP Act, 2008 gives partners limited liability, but a partner remains liable for their own wrongful acts. A company under the Companies Act, 2013 is a separate legal entity; members' liability is limited to the amount unpaid on their shares. The corporate veil can be lifted for fraud, tax evasion, or treating the company as a mere agent. Share capital can be issued partly paid, subject to the company's articles and the Act; there is no rule that it must be paid up within five years.
12-3.cost: Registration is online through the MCA V3 portal for a company or LLP, and through the GST and Udyam portals for tax and MSME registration. Government fees vary with authorised capital and state stamp duty. Ongoing bookkeeping, audit (where required) and tax filing cost money; a private company must file annual returns and audited accounts.
12-3.caveats: The limited-liability principle depends on separating company and personal money. Do not use the company account for personal expenses, and keep proper books. Do not inflate authorised capital for appearance; it increases fees and, for a company, the amount that can be called on shares. A private company must have at least two directors and two shareholders; a One Person Company has one. Check the current MCA fee and filing rules before you incorporate.
12-3.sources: Companies Act, 2013. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>; Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>; Indian Partnership Act, 1932. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

12-4.inPlainWords: If your name is on the register of members, the company treats you as the shareholder. You are liable for calls on your shares and, on winding up, for the unpaid amount. A private arrangement to hold shares for someone else can be a benami transaction: the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 makes benami property liable to confiscation and the arrangement void, and the Companies Act requires disclosure of beneficial ownership. Refuse requests to lend your name or your ID.
12-4.benefit: Being on the register makes you the legal shareholder with the duties that follow: paying calls, voting, and being a contributory on winding up. A person who holds shares for another can be a benami holder; the 1988 Act, as amended in 2016, prohibits benami transactions, allows attachment and confiscation of the property, and provides imprisonment. A company must also disclose its significant beneficial owners under section 90 of the Companies Act, 2013. A private nominee agreement does not override these rules, and the real owner may struggle to recover shares transferred to a bona fide purchaser for value.
12-4.cost: Zero expense. If someone asks you to lend your name, PAN, Aadhaar or DIN to hold shares, decline in writing.
12-4.caveats: A nominee is not the same as a beneficial owner; a nomination under the Companies Act is a mechanism for transmission of shares, not a transfer of ownership. If someone already holds shares for you, get independent legal advice before any transfer. Fines and prosecution under the benami law can fall on both the beneficial owner and the person who lends their name. The risks of being a nominal director are discussed in Section 8, item 28.
12-4.sources: Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Companies Act, 2013 (sections 88, 89, 90). <https://www.mca.gov.in/>; Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

12-5.title: No Indian franchise-disclosure statute: verify the trademark, the accounts and the contract before you pay
12-5.inPlainWords: India has no dedicated franchise law that forces a franchisor to disclose unit economics or to offer a cooling-off period. The relationship is governed by the contract, the Trade Marks Act, 1999, the Competition Act, 2002 and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Check that the brand's trademark is registered on the IP India portal, ask for audited accounts of company-owned outlets, and put termination, refund and cooling-off terms in the contract yourself.
12-5.benefit: Indian law does not impose the disclosure and registration regime that some countries apply to franchising. What you can do: search the trademark register at ipindia.gov.in; check the company's MCA filings for its financials and charges; ask for the franchise agreement, the fee schedule, the refund policy and the unit-level profit and loss accounts; and visit existing outlets. The Competition Act, 2002 can apply to anti-competitive tie-ins, and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 to misleading claims. A foreign franchisor also needs FEMA and RBI compliance for fees and royalties.
12-5.cost: No fee to search the trademark register. A lawyer's review of the agreement and the disclosures is worth the cost before you pay a franchise fee. Budget time to visit at least three outlets and to speak to franchisees who have left.
12-5.caveats: A trademark application is not a registration; check its status and class. A franchise agreement can make you liable for minimum purchases, territory quotas and penalties; read the termination and exit clauses. Do not pay a deposit before you see the agreement and the disclosure material. State consumer commissions can hear misrepresentation claims, but recovery takes time.
12-5.sources: Intellectual Property India, trademark search. <https://ipindia.gov.in/>; Competition Commission of India. <https://www.cci.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Ministry of Corporate Affairs, company filings. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>

12-6.title: Decide the name, address, activity and capital before you register; keep the incorporation documents
12-6.inPlainWords: Company and LLP registration in India runs through the MCA V3 portal with SPICe+ forms. You need a name, a registered office address, the objects, the capital, and the directors' or partners' KYC. After incorporation, register for GST if turnover crosses the threshold or you make inter-state supplies, register on Udyam for MSME benefits, and register under the state Shops and Establishments Act. Government fees vary; there is no single free one-day licence.
12-6.benefit: SPICe+ combines name reservation, incorporation, DIN, PAN, TAN and EPFO/ESIC registration for a company. An LLP uses the FiLLiP form. A proprietorship needs GST registration (if applicable), Udyam registration and a state Shops and Establishments registration; it has no separate incorporation. The registered office must be a real address with a no-objection certificate from the owner. A company must have at least two directors and two shareholders, and file annual returns and audited accounts.
12-6.cost: Government fees depend on authorised capital and state stamp duty; professional fees for drafting and filing are separate. GST registration is free. Udyam registration is free. A seal, letterhead and accounting cost extra. Do not pay an agent for a 'government approval' that is actually a private service.
12-6.caveats: A name reservation is not a trademark right; check the trademark register separately. A registered office must be able to receive notices. If your activity needs a licence (food, health, education, finance), incorporation does not replace it. The authorised capital is a ceiling, not a measure of credibility, and increasing it increases fees. Check the current MCA and GST rules before filing.
12-6.sources: Ministry of Corporate Affairs, SPICe+. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>; Goods and Services Tax Network. <https://www.gst.gov.in/>; Udyam registration. <https://udyamregistration.gov.in/>; Intellectual Property India. <https://ipindia.gov.in/>

12-7.title: Get the licence before you open — incorporation is not a licence
12-7.inPlainWords: A company or GST registration does not permit every activity. Food businesses need an FSSAI registration or licence; restaurants, hotels and shops need a state Shops and Establishments registration and often a trade licence; factories need registration under the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 and pollution consents; pharmacies need a drug licence. Opening without the required licence can lead to closure, penalties and, for some activities, prosecution.
12-7.benefit: The FSSAI licence depends on turnover and activity: a basic registration for small units, a state licence for medium units, and a central licence for large or multi-state units. A food business cannot operate without it. A factory must be registered with the registering officer under the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, which replaced the Factories Act, 1948 when it commenced on 21 November 2025, and must obtain consent from the State Pollution Control Board under the Water and Air Acts. A shop or commercial establishment registers under the state Shops and Establishments Act. A drug licence comes from the state drug controller. Each licence has its own renewal and display rules.
12-7.cost: Fees vary by state and by licence category. Budget for the licence fee, the inspection, and any required equipment or structural changes. Do not open for a trial run before the inspection; that is the most common and most expensive mistake.
12-7.caveats: Rules differ by state and by activity; check the state municipal and labour department pages. A licence for one premises does not cover another. Keep the licence displayed and renew it before expiry. If you change the activity or add a product line, check whether the licence covers it.
12-7.sources: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; Central Pollution Control Board. <https://cpcb.nic.in/>; Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. <https://labour.gov.in/labour-codes>; Ministry of Labour and Employment. <https://labour.gov.in/>; Ministry of Corporate Affairs. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>

12-8.title: Food rules in India: FSSAI registration or licence depends on what you make and sell
12-8.inPlainWords: If you make or sell food, you need an FSSAI registration or licence, and the category turns on turnover and activity. Under the FSSAI order of 13 March 2026, effective 1 April 2026, a basic registration covers turnover up to ₹1.5 crore, a state licence covers ₹1.5 crore to ₹50 crore, and a central licence is needed above ₹50 crore and for importers, exporters and units operating in more than one state. A petty food business or street vendor registers too, and the local municipal rules still apply.
12-8.benefit: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 and the FSSAI licensing regulations set the categories. The turnover thresholds were raised by the FSSAI order dated 13 March 2026, which took effect on 1 April 2026: basic registration up to ₹1.5 crore, state licence from ₹1.5 crore to ₹50 crore, central licence above ₹50 crore. A slaughterhouse needs an FSSAI licence and municipal clearance. Petty food businesses, including many street vendors, need a registration. The licence must be displayed at the premises, and operating without one can lead to closure, seizure and penalties under the Act.
12-8.cost: Fees depend on the category and the state. Keep the layout, water supply, drainage, pest control and staff medical checks in order before inspection. Do not pay an agent for a 'licence' without checking the FSSAI portal.
12-8.caveats: The threshold is revised from time to time, and the order of 13 March 2026 is the current one; check the FSSAI portal before you apply. A licence for one premises does not cover another. If you sell only packaged products made by someone else, you still need a registration or licence as a retailer. Check the current FSSAI rules and your municipal bye-laws.
12-8.sources: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, licensing and registration. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

12-9.title: Packaged food needs a compliant label: name, ingredients, quantity, date marking, veg mark and FSSAI licence number
12-9.inPlainWords: If you pack food for sale, it is packaged food and needs a label that follows the FSSAI Labelling and Display Regulations, 2020 and the Legal Metrology rules. The label must carry the product name, ingredients, net quantity, nutritional information, the veg or non-veg mark, date marking, allergen declaration, the manufacturer's name and address, and the FSSAI licence number. Loose food sold from a container still needs the name, date and seller details. A missing or false label can lead to seizure and penalties.
12-9.benefit: The FSSAI Labelling and Display Regulations, 2020 require, among other things: the name of the food; a list of ingredients in descending order; nutritional information per 100 g or 100 ml; the veg/non-veg logo; net quantity; date of manufacture or packing and best-before/use-by; the name and address of the manufacturer or packer; and the FSSAI licence number. The Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 add the MRP, quantity and consumer-care details. Imported food needs an importer's label. Front-of-pack nutrition labelling is being phased in; check the current FSSAI direction.
12-9.cost: Design and print costs depend on the run. Keep the licence number and the label artwork on file. The expensive mistake is printing a large run before the label is checked.
12-9.caveats: The label must match the product; a generic label with a different ingredient list is a misbranding risk. Dates must be in the prescribed format. If you repack or relabel, you may need your own licence. Check the current regulations and the Legal Metrology rules before printing.
12-9.sources: FSSAI, Labelling and Display Regulations. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs, Legal Metrology. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

12-10.title: Ordinary food must not claim to prevent or cure disease — on the pack, in ads, or in a live-stream script
12-10.inPlainWords: Packaged food, labels and advertisements must not claim that an ordinary food prevents or treats a disease. Those claims are reserved for licensed medicines, and even then only within the drug advertising rules. The FSS Act prohibits misleading claims, and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the CCPA can act on misleading advertisements. The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 separately prohibits disease claims for non-medicines.
12-10.benefit: Section 24 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 restricts advertisement and claims for food. The FSSAI's advertising and claims regulations set the conditions for nutrition and health claims. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 defines a misleading advertisement and allows the Central Consumer Protection Authority to order discontinuation and impose penalties. The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 prohibits advertisements of remedies for specified diseases. A claim that a snack 'cures diabetes' or 'prevents cancer' is not a clever marketing line; it is a regulatory risk.
12-10.cost: No cost to avoid the claim. Have a lawyer or a food consultant read the pack and the ad script before publication. Keep the substantiation for any nutrition claim.
12-10.caveats: 'Natural', 'immunity-boosting' and similar words can still be misleading if they imply a disease benefit. A disclaimer does not cure a false claim. Influencer and live-stream scripts are advertisements too. The exact claim rules depend on the product category; check the FSSAI regulations.
12-10.sources: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Central Consumer Protection Authority. <https://ccpa.gov.in/>; Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

12-11.title: Food safety offences can be criminal: unsafe or adulterated food is not just a fine
12-11.inPlainWords: Selling unsafe food is an offence under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The penalty depends on the harm: from a fine to imprisonment, and life imprisonment where death or grievous hurt results. Adulteration with a foreign substance, sale of diseased meat, and false labelling can also be prosecuted under the general criminal law. A food business owner cannot assume that a supplier's paperwork shifts all responsibility.
12-11.benefit: The FSS Act, 2006 creates offences for unsafe food (section 59), food containing extraneous matter (section 60), misbranded food (section 61) and misleading advertisement (section 24). Punishments range from fines to imprisonment, and the court can order compensation. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 contains offences for adulteration of food and cheating. The FSSAI can suspend or cancel a licence, seize stock and close the premises. Directors and managers can be prosecuted where the offence was committed with their consent or connivance.
12-11.cost: No cost to comply. Keep supplier invoices, licences, test reports and batch records. A recall plan and traceability records reduce the damage if something goes wrong.
12-11.caveats: The exact offence and punishment depend on the facts and the harm caused. A supplier's indemnity does not protect you from a criminal prosecution. If a customer reports illness, preserve the stock and records and take legal advice before making statements.
12-11.sources: Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

12-12.title: After registration, file your returns on time — a nil return is still a return
12-12.inPlainWords: A company, LLP, partnership or proprietorship must file its income-tax return even when there is no income, and a GST-registered business must file GST returns even when there are no sales. A company must also file annual accounts and the annual return with the MCA. Missing filings attract late fees, interest and, for a company, director disqualification and strike-off. A nil return is not optional.
12-12.benefit: Income-tax returns are due under the Income-tax Act, 2025, which replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961 from 1 April 2026; the due date depends on the entity and whether an audit applies. GST returns are due under the CGST Act, 2017: a normal taxpayer files GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B, and a composition dealer files CMP-08 and GSTR-4. A company files AOC-4 and MGT-7 with the MCA, and an LLP files Form 8 and Form 11. Late GST filing attracts a late fee and interest; late income-tax filing attracts a fee under section 428 of the 2025 Act and interest. Persistent default can lead to suspension or cancellation of GST registration and to director disqualification under section 164 of the Companies Act.
12-12.cost: The filing itself is free on the official portals. An accountant's fee is the real cost. Keep the portal credentials and the acknowledgement for every filing.
12-12.caveats: The due dates and fees change with the finance legislation and notifications. A nil GST return still has to be filed. Do not ignore a notice; reply on the portal within the deadline. If you have stopped trading, close the registration properly rather than letting returns lapse.
12-12.sources: Income Tax Department, e-filing. <https://www.incometax.gov.in/>; Goods and Services Tax Network. <https://www.gst.gov.in/>; Ministry of Corporate Affairs, MCA21. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>

12-13.title: Invoices must match real supplies; small businesses can use the composition and threshold schemes
12-13.inPlainWords: A GST invoice must describe an actual supply, with the GSTIN, invoice number, date, description, quantity, taxable value and tax. A composition dealer issues a bill of supply and cannot charge GST on it. Fake invoices to claim input tax credit are a serious offence: the department can deny the credit, impose a penalty and prosecute. Use the composition scheme or the threshold exemption only if you meet its conditions.
12-13.benefit: Under the CGST Act, 2017 a registered person must issue a tax invoice for a taxable supply, and a bill of supply for an exempt or composition supply. The composition scheme is available to small taxpayers below the notified turnover, with restrictions on inter-state supply and input tax credit. The threshold exemption means registration is not required below the notified turnover, subject to the conditions. Claiming input tax credit on a fake invoice can lead to reversal, penalty under section 122, and prosecution. E-invoicing applies above the notified turnover.
12-13.cost: Accounting software and a CA cost money; a fake invoice costs more. Keep the purchase order, invoice, e-way bill and payment trail for every transaction.
12-13.caveats: The thresholds and composition rates change. A composition dealer cannot claim input tax credit and cannot make inter-state taxable supplies. Do not accept a bill with a mismatched GSTIN or a supplier who cannot show the goods. Check the GST portal for the current limits.
12-13.sources: Goods and Services Tax Network. <https://www.gst.gov.in/>; Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs. <https://www.cbic.gov.in/>; CGST Act, 2017. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

12-14.title: No tax official asks for an OTP or a transfer to a private account — verify on the portal and report fraud on 1930
12-14.inPlainWords: The Income Tax Department does not ask for your bank password, card PIN, OTP or payment code over the phone, and it does not give you a private account to pay tax into. Verify any demand on the e-filing portal or with your assessing officer. If you have transferred money, call 1930 and file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in immediately; a quick report can freeze the funds.
12-14.benefit: Tax payments go through the e-filing portal, the authorised bank, or the GST portal; the department does not collect tax into a personal account. Phishing emails and calls impersonating tax officials are common. The Cyber Crime Coordination Centre runs the 1930 helpline and the cybercrime.gov.in portal for financial fraud. The Income Tax Department publishes alerts about fake refund and assessment notices on its portal. A genuine notice is visible in the e-filing account, and a genuine officer can be verified through the department's contact details.
12-14.cost: No cost. The few minutes spent verifying a demand on the portal are the cheapest protection. Report the fraud even if the amount is small.
12-14.caveats: A caller can spoof a number and use a fake letterhead. Do not click a link in an SMS or email; type the portal address yourself. A refund is credited to the bank account linked to the PAN, not to an account chosen by a caller. If you have shared an OTP, change the password and inform the bank at once.
12-14.sources: Income Tax Department. <https://www.incometax.gov.in/>; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, fraud awareness. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>

12-15.title: Write 'security deposit' or 'earnest money' deliberately; a penalty clause must be a reasonable pre-estimate
12-15.inPlainWords: Indian contract law does not give a 'deposit' an automatic double-return rule. Whether money is a security deposit, earnest money or an advance depends on the words and the purpose. A clause that fixes a penalty is enforceable only up to reasonable compensation under section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. If you allow credit, you are lending money; check the buyer before you do.
12-15.benefit: The Indian Contract Act, 1872 governs. Section 74 allows the court to award reasonable compensation for breach, whether or not a sum is named; a clause that is a penalty rather than a genuine pre-estimate can be reduced. A security deposit is usually refundable after the contract ends, subject to deductions; earnest money is forfeited if the buyer defaults, but the label is not conclusive. A seller cannot claim both a deposit and damages for the same loss if that would overcompensate. Credit terms are a separate contract of loan or sale on credit, and recovery depends on the buyer's solvency.
12-15.cost: No cost. Define the deposit, its refund conditions, and the deduction rules in writing. Before giving credit, check the buyer's MCA filings and credit record, and set a credit limit.
12-15.caveats: The words 'advance', 'deposit' and 'earnest money' are not statutory terms with fixed consequences; the contract and the facts decide. A court may adjust an excessive penalty. A cheque or promissory note is not a guarantee of payment. For recovery, a summary suit or commercial court may be available depending on the amount.
12-15.sources: Indian Contract Act, 1872 (sections 73, 74). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Corporate Affairs, company filings. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>; Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

12-16.title: Give a written appointment letter and register for ESIC and EPF — employees cannot waive statutory cover
12-16.inPlainWords: Indian law does not impose a 'double wages' penalty for a missing written contract, but an appointment letter is still essential to prove the wage, role and notice terms. An establishment covered by ESIC must register its employees within the prescribed period, and an establishment covered by EPFO must enrol eligible employees in the provident fund. An employee cannot validly waive statutory social-security cover. Keep the appointment letter, wage register and contribution records.
12-16.benefit: The Code on Wages, 2019 requires timely wage payment, wage slips and registers, and the state Shops and Establishments Acts require written particulars of employment. The Code on Social Security, 2020 and the ESIC and EPF schemes set the registration and contribution duties; the four labour codes commenced on 21 November 2025. ESIC generally covers a factory using power with ten or more employees and any other establishment with twenty or more, and some states have notified a lower threshold of ten for particular establishments; it covers employees within the wage ceiling, while EPFO generally covers establishments with twenty or more. A written contract that makes an employee waive ESIC or EPF is not a defence to a statutory claim. Failure to register or contribute can lead to damages, interest and prosecution.
12-16.cost: Employer contributions are a recurring cost; the employee's share is deducted from wages. The appointment letter and register cost nothing. Use the official ESIC and EPFO portals rather than an agent.
12-16.caveats: Coverage depends on the establishment's size, activity and state rules, and the wage ceiling changes. A consultant or contractor is not automatically an employee; misclassification can create liability. Keep the UAN and ESIC insurance number for each employee.
12-16.sources: Employees' State Insurance Corporation. <https://esic.gov.in/>; Employees' Provident Fund Organisation. <https://www.epfo.gov.in/>; Code on Social Security, 2020. <https://labour.gov.in/labour-codes>; Code on Wages, 2019. <https://labour.gov.in/labour-codes>

12-17.title: Pay wages on time and in full; put every raise, bonus and loan in writing
12-17.inPlainWords: Wages must be paid on the due date and in full, without unauthorised deductions. The Code on Wages, 2019 and the state Shops and Establishments Acts set the payment cycle and the limits on deductions. A verbal promise of a raise or bonus is hard to prove. If the employer lends money to an employee, use a written loan agreement with the amount, interest, repayment schedule and authorisation to deduct.
12-17.benefit: The Code on Wages, 2019 requires payment of wages within the prescribed time and restricts deductions to those authorised by law or the contract. Bonus is now Chapter IV of the Code on Wages, 2019, at sections 26 to 41, which replaced the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 when the Code commenced on 21 November 2025, and it applies to eligible establishments and employees. An employer cannot make an unauthorised deduction from wages to recover a loan; a written agreement and, where required, the employee's consent are needed. For an unpaid wage claim the route is the labour authority: a claim before the authority under the Code on Wages, 2019, which can order recovery, with an appeal to the appellate authority; a civil suit is possible but slower and costlier.
12-17.cost: No cost. Put the wage, the pay date and the deduction rules in the appointment letter. Record every raise with a signed letter. Do not run a personal loan through the salary account without paperwork.
12-17.caveats: The payment cycle and the deduction limits depend on the Code and the state rules. A bonus is statutory only for covered establishments; otherwise it is contractual. A loan agreement cannot authorise an illegal deduction. Keep the wage register and the bank statements.
12-17.sources: Code on Wages, 2019, including Chapter IV on bonus. <https://labour.gov.in/labour-codes>; Ministry of Labour and Employment. <https://labour.gov.in/>

cost: Just a few dozen to a few hundred yuan is needed
A few hundred to a few thousand rupees is needed

12-19.inPlainWords: The gap between one prototype and a thousand units is where the money goes. Yield decides your real unit cost. The supplier's minimum order quantity and payment terms decide how much cash you tie up. Inventory decides when that cash comes back. Some products also need a mandatory Indian certification or licence before they can be made or sold.
12-19.benefit: Yield is the share of a batch that is actually saleable; a low yield raises the true unit cost. The minimum order quantity and the advance payment set your working capital. Packaging, freight, GST and returns change the landed cost. In India, electronics may need BIS certification under the Compulsory Registration Scheme; packaged goods need Legal Metrology compliance; food needs FSSAI; drugs and cosmetics need a drug licence; and some products need a pollution consent. A prototype that has not been through these checks is not a product.
12-19.cost: A small prototype batch costs a few thousand rupees. Spend a few hours calculating yield, the supplier's minimum order and payment terms, the cash tied up in stock, packaging and freight, and the certification and trademark fees. The hard part is resisting the urge to skip this and start production.
12-19.caveats: Check the trademark register before you print packaging. Keep the design files and the licences. The certification list changes; check the BIS, FSSAI and Legal Metrology sites for your product. A certificate for one model does not cover a different model.
12-19.sources: Bureau of Indian Standards, CRS. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; FSSAI. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs, Legal Metrology. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Intellectual Property India. <https://ipindia.gov.in/>

12-20.title: Keep invoices and supplier records — selling counterfeit goods can be a crime even if an employee bought them
12-20.inPlainWords: Selling goods with a counterfeit trademark or pirated content is an offence under the Trademarks Act, 1999 and the Copyright Act, 1957, and can also be prosecuted as cheating or counterfeiting under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. 'I did not know' is not a complete defence where the price was obviously below market and the paperwork is missing. Keep the purchase contract, invoice, payment record, supplier GSTIN and authorisation for every batch.
12-20.benefit: The Trademarks Act, 1999 allows the owner to sue for infringement and passing off, and the court can order damages, accounts and delivery-up. The Copyright Act, 1957 provides criminal remedies for commercial infringement. The BNS, 2023 contains offences for cheating, forgery and counterfeiting. Customs and the police can seize infringing stock. A seller who can show lawful acquisition and identify the supplier may avoid some civil liability, but that defence depends on genuine records.
12-20.cost: No cost to keep records. For every batch, file the purchase order, invoice, payment proof, the supplier's GSTIN and licence, and the brand authorisation. Refuse stock offered at a price far below the market.
12-20.caveats: The threshold for prosecution and the remedy depend on the value and the facts. Destroying records after a complaint makes the position worse. If you suspect counterfeit stock, stop selling, preserve it and take legal advice before contacting the brand.
12-20.sources: Trademarks Act, 1999. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Copyright Act, 1957. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Intellectual Property India. <https://ipindia.gov.in/>

12-21.title: Changing colours or adding icons does not license someone else's artwork
12-21.inPlainWords: Copyright protects the artwork, photograph, font and design you copy. Changing the colour, background or a few icons does not create a new work or a licence. Using a character, a celebrity image or a font without permission can lead to a civil claim and, for commercial infringement, a criminal complaint. Trademark law separately prohibits a mark likely to confuse.
12-21.benefit: The Copyright Act, 1957 gives the owner the exclusive right to reproduce, adapt and communicate the work. A derivative work made without permission infringes. The Act provides civil remedies and criminal punishment for infringement; the exact threshold depends on the work and the commercial use. The Trademarks Act, 1999 protects a mark that is likely to deceive or cause confusion. The Designs Act, 2000 protects a registered design. Stock-image and font licences are limited to the stated use; a 'free' personal licence usually does not cover commercial packaging.
12-21.cost: A stock licence or a designer's fee costs far less than a claim. Keep the licence, the invoice and the designer's warranty for every image and font. Commission original artwork where the budget allows.
12-21.caveats: A licence can be limited by geography, print run, product and time. A font bundled with software is often not licensed for embedding or commercial print. A cease-and-desist letter is a warning; preserve the records and take legal advice.
12-21.sources: Copyright Act, 1957. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Trademarks Act, 1999. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Designs Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Intellectual Property India. <https://ipindia.gov.in/>

12-22.title: Follow your profession's protocol; the law protects a genuine emergency helper, not an improvised role
12-22.inPlainWords: Every regulated profession has its own escalation rules. A nurse must report a deterioration to the doctor and must question an unsafe medical order. An employee should not take on a decision outside their authority, even to help. In India, the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 protects a Good Samaritan who helps a road-accident victim from civil and criminal liability for acting in good faith; that protection is specific to road accidents, not a general licence to practise outside your training.
12-22.benefit: The Indian Nursing Council Act, 1947 and the state nursing rules govern nursing practice, and hospital protocols require escalation. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 protect a person who gives emergency care to a road-accident victim in good faith. Professional councils — the National Medical Commission for doctors, the Indian Nursing Council for nurses, state councils for other professions — can act on misconduct. Following the protocol protects both the patient and you.
12-22.cost: No cost. Read the escalation protocol and the scope of your role. Record what you observed and to whom you reported it. Ask for written instructions if an order is unclear.
12-22.caveats: The Good Samaritan protection is not a blanket immunity for every act in every setting. A professional is still judged by their training and the standard of care. Do not sign a record you know to be false, and do not accept a 'flexible' shortcut that bypasses the protocol. On who regulates nursing: the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023 is enacted, but the Commission had not been constituted by 2026, so the Indian Nursing Council remains the operative regulator for nurses and midwives in the meantime; check which body is acting before you reply to a notice.
12-22.sources: Indian Nursing Council. <https://indiannursingcouncil.org/>; National Medical Commission. <https://www.nmc.org.in/>; Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (section 134A). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

12-23.title: Close a business properly: strike off or liquidate, do not abandon the filings
12-23.inPlainWords: If a company has no assets or liabilities, it can apply for strike-off under section 248 of the Companies Act, 2013, in Form STK-2 under the Companies (Removal of Names of Companies from the Register of Companies) Rules, 2016. An LLP can apply for strike-off under the LLP Act. If debts exceed assets, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 provides for liquidation, and an individual can seek a fresh start or insolvency resolution under Part III. Abandoning annual filings leads to strike-off, director disqualification and penalties.
12-23.benefit: A company that has not commenced operations, or has ceased business, can apply to the Registrar in Form STK-2 after settling liabilities and obtaining the required no-objection certificates. The earlier fast-track exit route has been folded into the 2016 Rules, so use Form STK-2 and the current rules rather than the older circular. An LLP uses Form 24 and the LLP strike-off rules. The IBC, 2016 governs corporate insolvency resolution and liquidation, and Part III governs individuals and partnerships. A director of a company that fails to file returns for three consecutive years can be disqualified under section 164(2).
12-23.cost: Government fees and professional fees vary. A strike-off is cheaper than years of default. Liquidation costs more and takes longer. Budget for tax clearances and the final return.
12-23.caveats: Strike-off does not extinguish a creditor's right to sue in every case; a creditor can apply to restore the company. Do not move assets out of the company before the process; that can be void. An individual insolvency has a qualifying period and restrictions; take advice.
12-23.sources: Ministry of Corporate Affairs, strike-off. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India. <https://ibbi.gov.in/>; Companies Act, 2013. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; LLP Act, 2008. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>

12-24.title: Before paying an agency for store operations or 'zero-inventory' dropshipping, verify the company, the contract and the refund terms
12-24.inPlainWords: The pattern is an entry fee, then upgrades, supplier advances and 'unfreezing' deposits. The dashboard orders are often fake and the withdrawal is blocked. This is fraud, and it can be reported on 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in. Pay only to the company's bank account named in a written contract, and never to a personal account.
12-24.benefit: The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 require a marketplace to disclose the seller and the grievance officer, and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 covers misleading claims. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 covers cheating. The Cyber Crime Coordination Centre runs 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in for financial fraud. Fake reviews and manipulated ratings can also attract action under the consumer rules and the BIS standard for online reviews.
12-24.cost: No cost to verify. Before paying, check the company on MCA, get the GSTIN, get a written contract with a refund clause, and pay by bank transfer to the company account. A quick call to 1930 after a fraudulent transfer can freeze the funds.
12-24.caveats: A genuine agency can still deliver poor service; that is a contract dispute, not necessarily fraud. Keep the ads, the chat, the contract and the payment proof. Do not pay a 'tax' or 'security deposit' to release your own money.
12-24.sources: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>; Ministry of Corporate Affairs. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, unauthorised entities. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>

12-25.title: File the annual return and accounts every year — even a dormant company must file
12-25.inPlainWords: A company files AOC-4 (financial statements) and MGT-7 (annual return) with the MCA each year. An LLP files Form 8 and Form 11. A GST-registered business files its GST returns, and a proprietorship files its income-tax return. The dates are fixed by the Companies Act, the LLP Act and the tax rules. Missing them leads to late fees, director disqualification and strike-off.
12-25.benefit: Section 92 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the annual return, and section 129 the financial statements. AOC-4 is due within 30 days of the AGM, and MGT-7 within 60 days. An LLP files Form 8 within 30 days of the end of the financial year and Form 11 by 30 May. The MCA charges additional fees for late filing. A company that fails to file for three consecutive years can be struck off, and its directors disqualified under section 164(2).
12-25.cost: MCA filing fees depend on capital and delay. A CA's fee is the main cost. Keep the DIN, DSC and portal credentials active.
12-25.caveats: The AGM date and the filing dates depend on the company's financial year and the extension granted. A dormant company still files. Do not pay an unsolicited caller who offers to 'regularise' the filing without checking the portal.
12-25.sources: Ministry of Corporate Affairs, MCA21. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>; Companies Act, 2013. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; LLP Act, 2008. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>

12-26.title: Raise money privately only from people who know the business; a public offer needs SEBI and the Companies Act
12-26.inPlainWords: Taking money from relatives, friends and employees who know the business can be a private placement. Advertising to the public and promising a fixed return is different: a public offer of securities needs a prospectus and SEBI compliance, and a collective investment scheme needs SEBI registration. A private placement under section 42 of the Companies Act is limited to 200 persons in a financial year and cannot be advertised publicly. Promising guaranteed returns can amount to cheating or an unauthorised deposit-taking scheme.
12-26.benefit: Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 governs private placement: the offer must be made to identified persons, the money must be kept in a separate account, and the allotment must be filed with the ROC. A public issue needs a prospectus under the Act and SEBI regulations. The SEBI Act, 1992 and the CIS regulations prohibit unregistered collective investment schemes. The RBI's directions restrict unauthorised deposit-taking by non-banking entities. The BNS, 2023 covers cheating. A private placement memorandum does not make a public offer legal.
12-26.cost: Legal and compliance costs are real. A term sheet and a shareholders' agreement are cheaper than a rescission claim. Keep the list of investors and the board resolutions.
12-26.caveats: The 200-person limit and the definition of a private placement change; check the current rules. A 'loan' from many unrelated people with a promised return can look like a public deposit. Do not accept money before the paperwork is complete.
12-26.sources: Securities and Exchange Board of India. <https://www.sebi.gov.in/>; Companies Act, 2013 (section 42). <https://www.mca.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

12-27.title: Check the permitted use before you sign a commercial lease; a residential flat is not automatically a shop
12-27.inPlainWords: A lease does not change the permitted land use. Using a residential flat for a shop or restaurant needs the local municipal permission and, in a housing society, the society's no-objection certificate. A food business also needs premises that satisfy the FSSAI and municipal conditions, including ventilation and waste disposal. If the permission cannot be obtained, the lease should allow you to terminate and get the deposit back.
12-27.benefit: Municipal and town-planning laws, the state Shops and Establishments Act and local body bye-laws govern the permitted use of premises. A housing society's bye-laws and the apartment owners' association rules may restrict commercial activity. The FSSAI licence is tied to the premises and its layout. A landlord cannot by contract override a statutory prohibition on the use. If the premises are unauthorised for the intended use, the municipality can stop the business and the tenant may have a claim against the landlord.
12-27.cost: No cost to check. Before you pay a deposit, ask for the property tax receipt, the sanctioned plan, the society NOC and the municipal trade licence. Put a condition in the lease that the deposit is refunded if the licence is refused.
12-27.caveats: The position differs by state and by the type of property. A 'commercial' label in the lease does not prove the zoning. A restaurant with a chimney still needs the neighbours' and the society's clearance. Take a local lawyer's advice before signing.
12-27.sources: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. <https://mohua.gov.in/>; Food Safety and Standards Authority of India. <https://www.fssai.gov.in/>; state municipal laws (check your state). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

12-28.title: Write the partnership deed before the money moves: capital, profit share, salary and exit
12-28.inPlainWords: Without a written deed, the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 supplies the default rules. Every partner may take part in the business, profits are shared equally, and a partner is not entitled to a salary unless the deed says so. A partner can retire with notice, and the firm may dissolve. Put the capital, profit ratio, who manages, the salary, admission and exit, and dispute resolution in a signed deed.
12-28.benefit: The Indian Partnership Act, 1932 requires the relationship to be governed by the deed, and sections 11 to 13 set defaults: equally in profits, no salary without agreement, and every partner's right to take part. Section 32 governs retirement, and section 43 dissolution by notice. A partnership is not a separate legal person, so partners are personally liable for the firm's debts. An LLP under the LLP Act, 2008 gives limited liability but needs its own agreement and filings.
12-28.cost: A stamped deed and a CA's or lawyer's fee cost little compared with a dispute. Register the firm with the Registrar of Firms if you want the legal advantages of registration.
12-28.caveats: A deed cannot make one partner bear all the losses as against third parties, and it does not bind a creditor who did not agree. An unregistered firm has limited rights to sue. If you want limited liability, use an LLP or a company rather than a general partnership.
12-28.sources: Indian Partnership Act, 1932. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>; Ministry of Corporate Affairs. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>
